aiExplanation: This code counts the **minimum number of swaps** needed to reorder `nums` so the elements are sorted by their **digit sum** (ties broken by the number itself). First, each number is wrapped in a small tuple `[originalIndex, digitSum, value]` using the helper `sum`, which repeatedly peels off the last digit with `% 10` and `Math.floor(num / 10)`. The tuples are then sorted by digit sum, falling back to the raw value when sums match, so `sorted[i][0]` tells us which original position should end up at slot `i`. The outer `while (count !== last)` loop keeps making passes until a full pass performs no swaps; in each pass it walks the array and, whenever the tuple at slot `i` did not originally come from index `i`, it swaps it to the slot where it belongs via the `swap` helper and increments `count`. Each swap places at least one element in its final position, and repeating passes until nothing changes guarantees every element is settled, so `count` ends up being the minimum number of swaps required.

After sorting, `sorted[i][0]` is the original index of the element that belongs in slot `i`. The main loop uses the classic **cycle-sort** idea: for each position `i`, as long as the tuple sitting there did not come from index `i`, it swaps it into the slot matching its original index via `swap` and bumps `count`. Each swap permanently fixes one element, and the inner `while` keeps going until slot `i` holds the correct tuple, so a single pass over the array is enough. The loop applies **cycle sort**: for every index `i`, while the tuple at `i` is not the one that belongs there, it reads the target index `j = sorted[i][0]`, swaps the tuples at `i` and `j` inline using a `temp` variable, and increments `count`. aiExplanation: This is the most memory-efficient take on finding the **minimum swaps** to sort `nums` by **digit sum** (ties broken by value). Instead of building an array of tuples, it keeps two flat arrays: `sums`, where `sums[i]` is the digit sum of `nums[i]` computed inline with `num % 10` and `Math.floor(num / 10)`, and `indices`, which starts as `[0, 1, 2, ...]`. It then sorts `indices` by looking up `sums[a] - sums[b]`, and when that is zero the `||` falls through to `nums[a] - nums[b]` as the tie-breaker, so afterwards `indices[i]` names the original position that should occupy slot `i`. The final loop is **cycle sort** on `indices`: for each `i`, while `indices[i]` is not `i`, it swaps `indices[i]` with `indices[indices[i]]` in place and increments `count`, which moves one element into its correct spot every time. The result is the same minimum swap count as the earlier versions, but with only two small numeric arrays instead of one array of three-element tuples, which is why it uses noticeably less memory.
